title: Iran Offers 7-Day Deal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz, but US Remains Skeptical
summary:
Iran says it has a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway that about 18 ships pass through daily — within seven days. But the deal depends on the United States, and the two countries have failed to make peace before.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York on Friday that the conditions are already written into a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed on June 18. "The choice now rests with the United States," he said. The plan was delivered to the US through Qatar.

The 14-point MOU was designed to bring about a ceasefire and partially reopen the strait. It said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon, the US would end its naval blockade, and both sides would stop military operations on "all fronts." It also included sanctions relief and said Iran would help commercial ships pass safely.

But the agreement fell apart when both sides resumed strikes. The US and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on February 28. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf, and by blocking the strait. Iran has since attacked vessels it says tried to cross without authorization.

Iran's President, Masoud Pezeshkian, also said Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country. He rejected claims that Iran is developing a nuclear weapon, saying: "If they wish to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords."

Trump is privately skeptical that Iran will meet his demands, and has told staff he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day through the strait, with some days as low as nine vessels. Meanwhile, Yemen's Houthis — allied with Iran — have intensified attacks on oil exports in the Red Sea, adding more risk to the region.
why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz is a global chokepoint, so a blocked waterway can raise fuel, shipping and food prices for families thousands of miles away; and whether Iran's offer on nuclear inspections is accepted could decide if the region moves toward diplomacy or another round of war.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow channel between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman; roughly a fifth of the world's oil travels through it, which is why blocking it can raise fuel and food prices far beyond the Middle East. Iran (a large Middle Eastern country that has been under U.S. sanctions for decades) has seen repeated talks over its nuclear program collapse.

Qatar (a small, wealthy Gulf state that often acts as a go-between for Iran and Western countries) carried the latest proposal to Washington. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (the official in charge of Iran's diplomacy), presented the plan at the United Nations in New York.

The Houthis (an armed group that controls much of Yemen and is allied with Iran) have attacked ships in the Red Sea, another vital shipping route, adding a second front of risk. The IAEA (the International Atomic Energy Agency, the UN body that monitors nuclear programs) would be the organization carrying out inspections, which Iran's president now says it will allow.

perspectives.description: From Tehran's view, the offer is a serious, written path out of the crisis: a ceasefire, safe passage for ships, and permission for UN inspectors — a rare concession on the nuclear question. Qatar's mediation is presented as proof that quiet diplomacy can still produce results even between bitter enemies.

American officials and Trump himself doubt Iran will actually follow through, pointing out that the last MOU fell apart and that Iran has since attacked ships and blocked the strait. They argue that sanctions relief would reward broken promises and that military pressure is the only reliable tool.

Both sides are using the same chokepoint as a bargaining chip: Iran can strangle oil traffic, and the U.S. can strangle Iran's economy. That symmetry makes any agreement fragile, because each side can break it quickly and can also gain by waiting. Houthi attacks in the Red Sea make the shipping risk worse regardless of what Washington decides.

If the deal holds, oil shipping and prices could calm within weeks and the inspection offer might grow into a broader nuclear agreement. If it fails, the likely path is renewed airstrikes, an even longer blockade, and higher costs for countries that depend on Gulf oil — including many that have no say in the dispute.
